5. 9. SUBHASUTTAM. (99).

Young man, there are these five <term>nīvaraṇā</term> <gloss>hindrances</gloss>. Which five? The hindrance of sensual desire, the hindrance of ill-will, the hindrance of sloth and torpor, the hindrance of restlessness and worry, and the hindrance of doubt. These, young man, are the five hindrances. By these five hindrances, the Brahmin Pokkharasāti of the Opamañña clan, from Subhagavana, is obstructed, covered, blocked, and enveloped. That he should know, see, or realize for himself any state of being beyond that of human capacity, any distinction in the knowledge and vision of the noble ones—such a situation does not exist. 

There are these five <term>kāmaguṇā</term> <gloss>strands of sensual pleasure</gloss>, young man. Which five? Forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, pleasing, charming, lovely, associated with sensual desire, and provocative; sounds cognizable by the ear—and so on—scents cognizable by the nose, tastes cognizable by the tongue, and tangibles cognizable by the body that are desirable, pleasing, charming, lovely, associated with sensual desire, and provocative. These, young man, are the five strands of sensual pleasure. By these five strands of sensual pleasure, the Brahmin Pokkharasāti of the Opamañña clan, from Subhagavana, is bound, infatuated, and deeply attached, seeing no danger in them and lacking the wisdom of escape, he enjoys them. That he should know, see, or realize for himself any state of being beyond that of human capacity, any distinction in the knowledge and vision of the noble ones—such a situation does not exist. 

What do you think, young man? Between a fire that one might kindle by relying on grass and wood, or a fire that one might kindle without grass and wood, which fire would be more radiant, more brilliant, and more luminous?

If one were to kindle a fire without grass and wood, Master Gotama, that fire would be more radiant, more brilliant, and more luminous.

That is an impossible situation, young man, it is not possible to kindle a fire without grass and wood unless one possesses supernormal power. <summary>The Buddha identifies the five hindrances and five strands of sensual pleasure as obstacles that prevent the Brahmin Pokkharasāti from attaining higher knowledge, then uses a fire analogy to explain the nature of rapture.</summary>
